newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos's recruitment of ex-soldiers stirs storm.
newsitem.headline: Ramos's recruitment of ex-soldiers stirs storm.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos's appointment of formner army officers to key state posts, combined with moves to extend his term, has caused concern in a nation still haunted by the harsh rule of the Marcos era.

Ramos, a former general who spent 40 years in the army before becoming president, touched off a storm when he picked retired military chief General Arturo Enrile two weeks ago to head the powerful Transportation and Communications Department.
Enrile joined a growing list of former top army and police officers whom Ramos has recruited into a traditionally civilian bureaucracy to fill sensitive posts in the state apparatus.

There are now more than 60 such recruits, including five cabinet ministers, exercising control over the 115,000-member military, a national police force of 100,000 men as well as air, land and sea transportation and communications.
They also hold positions in the media, the power sector and agencies that control the state lottery and casinos, giving them access to rich sources of funds.

"The packing of the civil bureaucracy with military men masks its more disturbing aspect," said political analyst Amando Doronila. "President Ramos has staged a creeping coup on the civil service by installing officers in strategic offices that are usually the first targets of a lightning power seizure."

Enrile's appointment coincided with a campaign by a citizens group to amend the constitution to allow Ramos to run for re-election next year, ostensibly to ensure continuity in his reforms, which have dramatically turned the economy around.
Ramos's six-year term ends in June 1998, and the constitution limits presidents to one term.
His pledges to step down next year and his denials that he has a hidden political agenda have failed to calm nerves.

"The Filipinos have been badly burned by their experience with Ferdinand Marcos and his martial law regime...and so their extreme sensitivity to developments that smack of repeating the Marcos experience," Doronila wrote in the Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper on Sunday.

Former president Marcos's iron-fisted 1965-86 rule was marked by the invocation of martial law and jailing of political opponents. He was ousted in 1986 by the "People Power" revolution that swept Corazon Aquino to power.
Media reports that the campaign to amend the constitution was hatched in the presidential palace in a project identifing Ramos by the codename "Marlboro" have heightened anxieties.
"Maybe some people are just smoking too much," Ramos said of the reports.

Even the Roman Catholic Church has voiced alarm. It has circulated letters nationwide warning that extending Ramos's term could pave the way for the rise of another Marcos, who was ousted in a 1986 popular revolt after 20 years in power.
"What I am afraid of is that now there is a network of vital and strategic government agencies that is a potential instrument for state control," said ex-armed forces chief Rodolfo Biazon.
The Inquirer newspaper said in an editorial that the campaign to change the constitution and the appointment of army men to the bureaucracy could provoke political instability.
"It is polarising the nation into fiercely opposing camps," it said, calling the former generals Ramos's "Trojan horses".

State university political science professor Alex Magno suggested Ramos had no choice but to recruit army men known for their administrative skills because it was difficult to lure private sector executives into a bureaucracy offering low pay.
"I am looking at this more in terms of market forces at work," Magno said. "I am sure there is no military conspiracy."
But another analyst, Felipe Miranda, said: "You give these people the kind of feel for political power beyond the normal term limits and then you might be tempting the fates."
